strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: the mismatch between standard caption-style benchmarks and diverse real-world user queries (conversational, reformulation, and exclusionary) in text-audio retrieval.

The data leakage analysis regarding WavCaps overlap with AudioCaps and Clotho is thorough and provides valuable community awareness, supported by clean evaluation on the uncontaminated MECAT benchmark.

The methodology for evaluating exclusionary queries is sound and well-formulated, introducing sensible hard-negative mining (acoustic similarity + semantic dissimilarity) alongside informative discrimination metrics (HNSR, Delta-Rank, TFR).
Extensive experimentation across multiple backbone scales (Nemotron-3B, Qwen2.5-Omni-3B, and 7B), accompanied by detailed efficiency and latency profiling.
weaknesses: On standard text-to-audio (T2A) retrieval and several positive UIQ categories (e.g., question, keyphrase, paraphrase), OEA is generally on par with or outperformed by M2D-CLAP; the primary performance gains are concentrated in text-to-text (T2T) and negative discrimination.

The architectural approach—applying LoRA adaptation with modality projection heads and symmetric InfoNCE loss on top of frozen multimodal LLM backbones—is fairly standard and offers limited technical novelty.

The UIQ benchmark relies predominantly on synthetic generation from a single LLM (GPT-5.1) with length constraints; while small-scale human validation is conducted on 75 samples, it may still not fully capture the idiosyncratic noise and distributions of natural user search logs.
Significant inference memory overhead (11.5–18.3 GB peak GPU memory vs. <1 GB for CLAP baselines), which poses practical hurdles for resource-constrained or edge deployment.

strengths: The paper addresses a critical and timely problem in audio-language retrieval: the discrepancy between descriptive, caption-style benchmark queries and realistic, diverse user search intents (conversational questions, imperatives, keyphrases, and exclusions).

Thorough and commendable data leakage analysis demonstrating the extensive contamination between WavCaps and standard evaluation benchmarks (AudioCaps and Clotho), coupled with evaluation on the leakage-free MECAT benchmark to ensure genuine generalization.

Well-motivated evaluation methodology for exclusionary queries, including a sensible hard negative mining pipeline and discrimination metrics (HNSR, TFR, Δ-Rank) that properly evaluate distractor suppression beyond standard top-k recall.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple model scales and backbones (Nemotron-3B, Qwen2.5-Omni-3B/7B), providing strong evidence that LLM backbones excel at instruction/command parsing, text-to-text semantic matching, and handling negation.
Extensive appendix detailing implementation specifics, prompt templates, human and LLM evaluation agreements, and latency/memory profiling.
weaknesses: The architectural novelty is relatively incremental; fine-tuning existing native audio LLMs via LoRA with standard symmetric InfoNCE contrastive loss is conventional in modern multimodal representation learning.

Significant parameter and compute disparity between OEA (3B to 7B parameters, 11–18 GB GPU memory) and baseline CLAP models (89M to 158M parameters, <1 GB GPU memory). Despite the parameter advantage, M2D-CLAP remains superior on standard AudioCaps T2A recall and on three out of four positive UIQ query types.

All UIQ benchmarks rely on synthetic generation via a single commercial LLM (GPT-5.1) under strict length constraints (±2 words of the caption). While human validation was conducted on a sample, real user search query logs (e.g., from Freesound) may exhibit patterns not fully captured by length-constrained synthetic rewrites.

strengths: Important data leakage analysis: The systematic analysis of training-test contamination between WavCaps and common evaluation benchmarks (17.7% AudioCaps test overlap, 61.0% Clotho overlap) exposes a critical evaluation flaw in existing literature and establishes cleaner benchmarking practices.

Well-motivated benchmark and evaluation protocol: The User-Intent Query (UIQ) taxonomy addresses the clear mismatch between training captions and real-world search interactions (e.g., conversational, imperative, and exclusionary formulations), supported by human validation and length controls.

Principled hard negative evaluation: The paper correctly identifies that standard recall metrics fail to capture distractor suppression in exclusionary search and proposes meaningful, purpose-built discrimination metrics (HNSR@k, TFR, and Delta-Rank).
Comprehensive empirical study: The authors evaluate multiple multimodal LLM families (Qwen2.5-Omni, Nemotron) across scales (3B, 7B) and include detailed efficiency and inference latency profiling.
weaknesses: Mixed performance gains on the primary T2A task: Omni-Embed-Audio does not uniformly outperform the state-of-the-art dual-encoder baseline (M2D-CLAP) on standard text-to-audio retrieval. M2D-CLAP remains superior on AudioCaps and across multiple UIQ query types (Question, Keyphrase, Paraphrase, and overall average UIQ R@5), with OEA's primary advantages concentrated in text-to-text (T2T) and hard negative discrimination.

Limited architectural novelty: Adapting pre-trained multimodal LLMs using LoRA and InfoNCE contrastive loss with mean pooling is largely standard practice adapted from recent multimodal and text embedding literature.

Potential synthetic generation artifacts: While the authors conduct human validation on a small subset (75 samples) and control for length, generating UIQ queries via a single proprietary LLM (GPT-5.1) may introduce stylistic priors that could subtly bias retrieval behavior compared to organic search logs.

High resource and memory footprint: Despite offline amortization of audio embeddings, the 3B-7B parameter backbones incur substantial memory footprints (11.5–18.3 GB GPU VRAM vs. <1 GB for CLAP models) and noticeably higher audio encoding latency, limiting deployment in constrained environments.

strengths: Rigorous data leakage and contamination analysis: The paper explicitly quantifies audio and metadata overlap between common pretraining corpora (WavCaps) and evaluation benchmarks (AudioCaps, Clotho), and validates generalization on the uncontaminated MECAT dataset.

Comprehensive and intellectually honest mechanistic ablations: Appendix O systematically unpacks the factors driving hard negative discrimination (audio embedding separability vs. contextual word order sensitivity) using paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests and cross-model shuffle controls, acknowledging where OEA behaves identically to baseline text encoders.

Well-motivated benchmark extension: The introduction of the User-Intent Queries (UIQ) taxonomy and hard-negative suppression metrics (HNSR, TFR, Delta-Rank) addresses real-world search variations (commands, keyphrases, exclusionary negation) that are not captured by standard caption-style benchmarks.

Strong performance on text-to-text (T2T) retrieval and imperative/exclusionary queries: Demonstrates clear utility for caption-based audio retrieval pipelines and command-driven conversational search interfaces.
weaknesses: Substantial computational overhead: Compared to specialized dual-encoder CLAP architectures, OEA incurs significantly higher audio encoding latency (163–666 ms vs. 31–107 ms) and GPU memory footprint (11.5–18.3 GB vs. ~0.6–0.7 GB), which may hinder deployment in high-throughput audio indexing settings.

Mixed baseline text-to-audio (T2A) performance: On standard T2A benchmarks like AudioCaps, M2D-CLAP noticeably outperforms OEA (e.g., 77.13% vs. 72.64% R@5), indicating that scaling to multi-billion parameter LLM backbones does not yield universal improvements over dedicated contrastive audio models.

Limited human validation sample size for UIQ: While the synthetic generation pipeline using GPT-5.1 is reasonably constrained, only 75 out of 13,053 queries were audited by human raters, leaving potential synthetic distribution shifts mostly unchecked across the full benchmark.

Diminishing returns across model scales: Moving from 3B to 7B parameters yields marginal or negative gains across several retrieval metrics, suggesting that contrastive alignment dynamics become a bottleneck rather than backbone parameter capacity.

strengths: Critically addresses a realistic information retrieval gap: moving beyond stylized caption-like queries in audio retrieval to evaluate user-intent query types (questions, commands, keyphrases, paraphrases, and exclusionary queries).

Exceptional methodological honesty and thoroughness in the ablation study (Appendix O): instead of hand-waving about 'LLM reasoning', the authors run rigorous counterfactual tests (audio distance, negation stripping, word shuffling) and demonstrate that the discrimination gains stem primarily from audio-space separation rather than an OEA-specific textual negation mechanism.
Careful data contamination analysis uncovering substantial test set overlaps in common audio benchmarks (AudioCaps and Clotho in WavCaps) and properly utilizing MECAT as an uncontaminated testbed.

Comprehensive experimental setup across multiple model backbones (Nemotron-3B, Qwen-3B, Qwen-7B), showcasing parameter-efficient adaptation (LoRA) and outstanding performance on text-to-text retrieval and hard negative distractor suppression.
weaknesses: Text-to-audio (T2A) retrieval performance does not universally beat dedicated contrastive models like M2D-CLAP (e.g., M2D-CLAP maintains an advantage on AudioCaps R@k and overall average UIQ R@5).

Inference latency and memory footprint are substantially higher than lightweight dual-encoder CLAP baselines, making real-time audio indexing or on-device scaling considerably more demanding despite LoRA parameter efficiency during training.

The UIQ benchmark generation relies on a single proprietary LLM (GPT-5.1) constrained to original vocabulary, and the human validation is conducted on a relatively small sample (75 query sets), leaving open how well it mirrors unstructured, noisy real-world search query logs.

strengths: Principled and thorough methodology: The paper introduces Omni-Embed-Audio (OEA), adapting multimodal LLMs with native audio understanding via LoRA for cross-modal audio-text retrieval, moving beyond traditional dual-encoder CLAP architectures.

Comprehensive and realistic evaluation benchmark: The introduction of User-Intent Queries (UIQs) across five diverse formulations (questions, imperatives, tags, paraphrases, and negative queries) addresses critical benchmark limitations of conventional caption-style queries.

Rigorous data leakage analysis: The authors provide an exemplary investigation into pretraining contamination between WavCaps and standard evaluation benchmarks (AudioCaps and Clotho), demonstrating genuine evaluation rigor by testing on an uncontaminated dataset (MECAT).

Exemplary mechanism ablations and scientific honesty: Appendix O provides deep mechanistic insight into hard-negative discrimination, dissecting audio-space separation versus text-side compositional reasoning, and showing through cross-model controls that order sensitivity is general across transformers while OEA's primary differentiator lies in audio-side representation separation.
Clear, well-structured presentation with extensive baseline comparisons, statistical significance tests, and validation of generated query benchmarks via human and LLM annotations.
weaknesses: Mixed Text-to-Audio (T2A) retrieval gains: On standard T2A retrieval benchmarks, OEA does not consistently outperform state-of-the-art CLAP baselines (e.g., M2D-CLAP performs significantly better on AudioCaps R@5, 77.13% vs 72.64%), with OEA's primary advantages concentrating in T2T and specific subset formulations (imperative, exclusionary discrimination).

Computational overhead and deployment complexity: As shown in Table 16, LLM backbones require substantially greater inference latency and GPU memory (peak memory 11.5–18.3 GB vs ~0.6–0.7 GB for CLAP), especially for audio encoding, limiting suitability for resource-constrained environments.

Reliance on synthetic query generation: Although sample validation was performed, the UIQ benchmark relies on queries generated by a proprietary LLM (GPT-5.1) rather than mined real-world user search queries from production search logs, which may carry subtle synthetic distribution characteristics.
